title: Word2Vec and GloVe
oneLiner: Two famous ways to learn word vectors from plain text: guess a word's neighbours (Word2Vec) or fit the whole table of which words appear together (GloVe).

what.html:
Word2Vec learns word vectors by playing a guessing game over billions of words: given a word, which words are likely to be nearby? To make it fast, it turns the guess into "is this pair of words real, or a random fake?" GloVe first counts how often every pair of words appears together across the whole text, then finds vectors whose combinations reproduce those counts.

Everyday versionYou can get to know people at a party by noticing who they usually stand next to; people who keep similar company end up "close" in your mental map.

why.html:
• They made good word vectors cheap to learn from huge amounts of text.
  • The vectors capture similarity and even analogies.
  • Their tricks (self-supervision, negative sampling) are still used in modern models.

how.title: Directions that mean something
how.html: One-hot vectors make every word equally unrelated. Learned vectors turn relations into directions: king − man + woman lands near queen.

how.title: Guess the neighbours
how.html: Slide a window over the text. Each word and each nearby word form a training pair: from "brown" predict "quick", "fox"… Words used in similar company end up with similar vectors.

how.title: Too many words to choose from
how.html: Picking the right neighbour among 100,000 words for every pair is far too slow.

how.title: Real or fake?
how.html: Instead, check one real pair against a few random fake pairs: pull real neighbours together, push fake ones apart. For "king": real neighbour "rules" (score 0.29), fake "table" (0.10); one update nudges king toward rules and away from table.

how.title: Which fakes, which words
how.html: Pick fake words in proportion to frequency raised to 0.75 (rare words get a little boost), and randomly skip very common words like "the" while training.

how.title: The reverse direction
how.html: CBOW does the opposite: average the neighbours and guess the missing middle word. Faster; skip-gram is better for rare words.

how.title: GloVe: count first
how.html: Count every pair of words across the whole corpus. Ratios tell meaning: "solid" appears with "ice" about 9 times more than with "steam"; "water" with both; "fashion" with neither.

how.title: GloVe: fit the counts
how.html: Find vectors so that (word vector · context vector + two biases) ≈ log(count), giving rare pairs little weight and capping very common ones.

demo.html: Press Play to train Word2Vec on mixed text about royalty and food. Starting from random points, the two topics drift apart, learned only from which words appeared near each other.

example.html:
One GloVe step. For "cat" and "milk", the model predicts 0.63 but the log count is 3: an error of −2.37. Weighted by 0.8, the loss is 4.49. The update moves both vectors and the bias so the next prediction is higher: v becomes [0.519, 0.371], u [0.195, 0.938], b 0.29.

Supplementary Word2Vec with negative sampling turns out to be secretly factorising a word–context PMI matrix, so the "predict" and "count" approaches are closer than they look.

misunderstandings: They're approximate and reflect corpus biases.
takeaways: One-hot fails; learned vectors encode relations (king − man + woman ≈ queen).
Skip-gram predicts neighbours; full softmax is too costly.
Negative sampling: real vs K fake pairs with σ (worked update).
Noise ∝ count^0.75; subsample frequent words; CBOW is the reverse.
GloVe fits log co-occurrence counts with weighted least squares (worked J = 4.49).
thirty: One-hot vectors are orthogonal and carry no similarity; Word2Vec learns dense vectors where relations are offsets (king − man + woman ≈ queen). Skip-gram uses each (centre, context) pair in a window to train two vector sets via softmax P(c|w), but the softmax over V words is a bottleneck. Negative sampling replaces it with binary classification: −log σ(v·u⁺) − Σ log σ(−v·u⁻), giving push–pull updates; negatives come from counts^0.75 and frequent words are subsampled (1 − √(t/f)). Worked: v = [0.1, 0.3], u⁺ = [0.2, 0.9], u⁻ = [0.7, 0.1], α = 0.1 → v ≈ [0.072, 0.334]. CBOW predicts the centre from averaged contexts. GloVe uses global co-occurrence counts, motivated by probability ratios (ice/steam), and minimises Σ f(Xᵢⱼ)(vᵢ·uⱼ + bᵢ + b̃ⱼ − log Xᵢⱼ)² (worked J = 4.49, v → [0.519, 0.371]).
